title: What America Can Learn from England’s Education Revolution https://www.nationalreview.com/2026/09/what-america-can-learn-from-englands-education-revolution/
author: Robert Pondiscio and Nick Gibb
summary: Robert Pondiscio and former English schools minister Nick Gibb argue that England, a large, diverse democracy that shares America's language and many of its education debates, cannot be explained away the way Americans dismiss Singapore or Finland. They point to England's strong new PISA results and rising PIRLS rankings, with some of the largest gains among its lowest performers, while U.S. reading scores fell sharply. England's reforms began with synthetic phonics and a universal phonics screening check, but the authors warn that Americans risk learning only half the lesson, since phonics is just the starting line. Drawing on E. D. Hirsch Jr., whose ideas shaped England's 2014 National Curriculum, they argue that knowledge is a prerequisite for comprehension and critical thinking. Contrasting England with Scotland and Wales, they urge American states, with Texas as an early example, to pursue coherent, knowledge-rich curriculum, standards, and assessment.
points: The share of English six-year-olds meeting the phonics standard rose from 58 percent in 2012 to 82 percent in 2018.
England rose from tenth in PIRLS in 2011 to fourth in 2021 while U.S. performance stayed flat.
Hirsch's argument that knowledge is a prerequisite for comprehension shaped England's 2014 National Curriculum.
Scotland and Wales, which favored broad competencies over specified knowledge, diverged markedly from England after 2010.
Texas is building an England-inspired system of phonics, knowledge-rich materials, standards, and aligned assessment.
quotes: England, however, is harder to explain away. It’s a large, diverse democracy that shares our native language.
The percentage of six-year-olds meeting expected standards rose from 58 percent in 2012 to 82 percent in 2018 — compelling evidence that these reforms are bearing fruit.
But there is a danger that Americans will learn only half of England’s lesson. Namely, that American educators have oversimplified reading instruction. Phonics is just the starting line.
Schools that do not ensure that children from low-income families acquire that wide range of knowledge across a broad curriculum are functionally imposing illiteracy on them.
In essence, England began to treat reading as both a phonics code to be mastered and a body of knowledge to be taught and shared.

Rather, it changed things by taking a set of ideas about how children learn seriously enough to turn them into public policy — and by rigorously sticking with those ideas long enough for them to reach classrooms.
America need not become England. But its states could do worse than relearn some of the lessons Americans taught the English in the first place.
